title: Shelter hotels that also lobby or appear in campaign filings
question: Do the hotels paid under the shelter programme, or the owners named for them, also appear as lobbyists’ clients or in campaign contribution filings?
finding: Of 30 hotel payees, 5 appear, under their own name or a registered owner’s, as a registered lobbyist’s client (HTL 587: 23 contacts, $5,506 paid to lobbyists; Nob Hill Hotel: 27 contacts, $2,786 paid to lobbyists; Intercontinental San Francisco: 2 contacts, $100 paid to lobbyists; Cova Hotel: 1 contact, $3,500 paid to lobbyists; Hotel Epik: 5 contacts, $553 paid to lobbyists) and 12 appear in campaign filings since 2015, as a contributor or as a contributor’s employer, $34,900 in all. Most of the lobbying concerned permits. For 2 hotels the lobbyist reported contacts about the City’s own use of the property: HTL 587 (23 contacts; Homelessness and Supportive Housing, 2020: “Lease Negotiations”); Nob Hill Hotel (1 contact; Mayor, 2021: “City's Purchase of Client Property”). Measured against the sums paid for rooms the money is very small. These are matches on a name, and a contact is on file only because the lobbyist reported it.
how: Each hotel payee, every name the project’s owner-groups tie to it, and the owner named in its damage settlement were looked up, by exact normalized name, among the clients in the Ethics Commission’s lobbyist activity file (contacts with officials and payments to lobbyists) and in itemized contributions received by San Francisco committees since 2015 (the contributor’s own name where no first name is given, or the employer a contributor stated). Amended campaign filings are counted once. Contributors are not named; only counts and dollars are shown. A contact is counted as about the City’s use of the property when it was with the homelessness department or the lobbyist’s own description speaks of a lease, a purchase or shelter; the description is quoted in up to 12 words.
limits: A hotel hiring a lobbyist is ordinary: most of the subjects reported here are permits, and an owner who sends a registered lobbyist to negotiate a lease with a department is doing so in the open, which is why the contact is on file. A contribution that names a hotel as the donor’s employer is the donor’s own gift. Matching on names misses owners who give or lobby through a parent company, a manager or a principal, since the files on disk do not name the people behind each owning company, and it can join two businesses that share a common name. What would settle it: the owners of record of each hotel company (State business filings), set against the same lobbying and campaign files.
